prompt.context: Our client is a major convenience store chain with 5,000 stores in the US and $25B in annual revenues. About one year ago their CEO hired our firm to help increase profits. Since then, we have worked with the client to aggressively control costs through negotiating larger discounts from suppliers, restructuring the client's labor force, and cutting other operating expenses by 10%. As a result of our work, our partners believe there is little room for cost reductions going forward.
prompt.question: How else can we increase profits for our client?

clarifying_info.a: There are 4 major companies (including the client) in the industry that control 95% of the market. Each has a roughly similar share of the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is the client open to expanding or changing its product line?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client is not interested in expanding or changing the product line.
No, the client does not want to expand internationally due to logistical concerns.
We studied possible M&A activities, but there are no desirable targets.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client charge different prices across stores or geographies?
clarifying_info.a: The client charges the same price per item in each of its stores — no difference between prices of one item in Manhattan versus Durham.

clarifying_info.q: How loyal are pain reliever brand customers?
clarifying_info.a: Consumers consider Motrin and Tylenol to be very different brands, with each having very loyal customers. It would take a substantial change in price of one brand to convince customers to switch to the other. Buyers of both brands would consider the store brand product, however they feel it is a slightly inferior product and would need to be incentivized to do so.

clarifying_info.q: Do Advil and Motrin suppliers charge different prices to different chains?
clarifying_info.a: No, Advil and Motrin suppliers charge the same price to every convenience store chain.

clarifying_info.q: Are other costs (overhead, etc.) the same across chains?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, all other costs should be considered the same across the 4 major chains.

exhibits.title: Products Sold by Client
exhibits.shows: A table showing four product categories sold by the client, with Total Client Sales and Total Scan Margin (profit margin including producer funding) and Price Elasticity for each category.

exhibits.title: Convenience Store Industry Food & Beverage Sales
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the client and three competitors on Average Price/Unit, Total Unit Volume, Total $ Sales, and Share in the Food & Beverage segment. Some cells are blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Client Pain Reliever Sales
exhibits.shows: A table showing Total $ Sales, Price/Unit, and Cost/Unit for three pain reliever brands sold by the client. Profit/Unit, Total Units, and Total Profit are blank for the candidate to calculate.

exhibits.title: Convenience Store Pain Reliever Prices
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the client's price versus the average competitor price for each pain reliever brand.

exhibits.title: Pain Reliever Market Share $ by Brand
exhibits.shows: A chart showing dollar market share split between the client and 3 competitors for each of three pain reliever brands (Advil, Motrin, Store Brand).

framework: Since costs have already been aggressively reduced, focus entirely on revenue levers
Revenue = Price × Volume × Mix — investigate each dimension
Assess product categories by sales, margin, and price elasticity to prioritize
Investigate Food & Beverage (largest scan margin, highest elasticity) and Pain Relievers (lowest margin, most inelastic) as priority segments
For each segment, compare client pricing and volume/share to competitors to identify specific opportunities
Synthesize findings into a concrete pricing or mix recommendation

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, which product categories should the team prioritize and why?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies Pain Relievers (lowest scan margin implied, most inelastic demand at 0.3 — hardest to lose customers if price rises, so opportunity to raise prices) and Food & Beverage (largest scan margin at $3B, large revenue base at $9B — protect and grow this). Cleaning Products and Other have smaller absolute margins and are less strategically interesting. Candidate should note that low price elasticity in Pain Relievers means price increases won't significantly reduce volume.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what does the Food & Beverage competitive data tell us, and what is the client's unit volume and market share?
questions.guidance: Client has the highest price per unit ($1.50) but the lowest market share. Candidate should calculate client's unit volume and share, then conclude there is little room to raise prices further — and should redirect attention to Pain Relievers.

math.setup: Client Total $ Sales = Price/Unit × Unit Volume; also derive Competitor 1 price and missing $ Sales. Market share = client units / total units.
steps: Client market share = 6B / 36B = ~18% (lowest among all competitors)
math.answer: Client has 18% volume share — lowest in the industry — and the highest price per unit. Raising prices further would likely lose more volume. Food & Beverage is not the solution.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate each brand's profit per unit, total units sold, and total profit for the client's pain reliever portfolio.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute profit per unit (Price minus Cost), total units (Total $ Sales divided by Price), and total profit (Profit per unit times total units). Key insight: Advil dominates revenue ($8B) but has by far the lowest profit per unit ($0.20). Store Brand has the highest profit per unit ($0.70) but low volume. This raises the question of whether prices should be raised or mix shifted.

math.setup: Profit/Unit = Price/Unit - Cost/Unit; Total Units = Total $ Sales / Price/Unit; Total Profit = Profit/Unit × Total Units
steps: Store Brand: Profit/unit = $1.99 - $1.29 = $0.70; Units = $1B / $1.99 ≈ 500M; Total Profit = $0.70 × 500M = $0.35B
math.answer: Advil generates the most total profit ($0.40B) but has the lowest margin per unit ($0.20). Store Brand has the highest margin per unit ($0.70). Total pain reliever profit is approximately $0.85B.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 4 shows competitor pain reliever prices. What does this reveal, and what should we investigate next?
questions.guidance: Client prices Advil at $3.99 vs. competitor average of $4.69 — a $0.70 gap. Motrin is priced the same as competitors. Store Brand is priced slightly higher than competitors ($1.99 vs. $1.89). The key anomaly is Advil: the client is substantially underpricing relative to competition. A strong candidate asks for market share data to understand whether this low price is driving disproportionate volume.

math.setup: Price gap = Competitor Average - Client Price
math.answer: Client is significantly underpricing Advil by $0.70/unit relative to competitors. This is the largest anomaly and warrants investigation into whether volume justifies it.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 5 shows pain reliever market share by brand. What is the recommendation?
questions.guidance: Client holds 90% dollar share of Advil sales in the convenience store channel. Given that Advil has highly loyal customers unlikely to switch brands, and given that competitors charge $0.70 more per unit without losing share, the client should raise the price of Advil closer to the competitor level. Even a partial increase would generate significant profit uplift given ~2B units sold. Excellent candidates will also note: (1) potential to incentivize customers toward Store Brand (higher margin per unit), and (2) the insight that uniform pricing across all 5,000 stores is a missed opportunity — higher-cost markets (e.g., Manhattan) could bear higher prices.

math.setup: Illustrative profit impact of raising Advil price
steps: Current Advil profit/unit = $0.20; current total profit = $0.40B
If price raised by $0.50 (to $4.49, still below competitor avg of $4.69): new profit/unit = $0.70
Assume minimal volume loss given brand loyalty and 90% market share: new total profit ≈ $0.70 × 2B = $1.40B
math.answer: Raising Advil price by ~$0.50/unit could increase total pain reliever profit from ~$0.85B to ~$1.85B, an uplift of ~$1.0B, while risking minimal volume loss given brand loyalty and dominant market share.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond Pain Relievers and Food & Beverage, what other revenue or profit levers could the client explore?

categories.name: Pricing strategy
ideas: Implement geographic/market-based pricing (e.g., higher prices in high-cost cities like Manhattan)
Introduce tiered promotions or loyalty pricing to drive volume without uniform price cuts
Re-examine Store Brand pricing relative to national brands to capture more margin

categories.name: Product mix optimization
ideas: Shift marketing and shelf space toward Store Brand pain relievers which have highest profit per unit
Rationalize SKUs in low-margin categories to reduce complexity

categories.name: Revenue per transaction
ideas: Upsell or bundle complementary items at checkout
Increase basket size through store layout improvements or bundled promotions

categories.name: Customer loyalty and traffic
ideas: Launch or enhance a loyalty program to increase visit frequency
Partner with fuel stations or other foot-traffic generators

categories.name: Ancillary revenue
ideas: Increase advertising/media revenue from supplier co-marketing programs
Lease shelf space or endcaps to suppliers at premium rates

recommendation: Raise the price of Advil from $3.99 toward the competitor average of $4.69, starting with an increase of approximately $0.50/unit
Given Advil's 90% market share in the convenience store channel and consumers' strong brand loyalty, volume loss should be minimal — this could generate approximately $1B in additional annual profit
In parallel, explore geographic pricing differentiation (charge more in high-cost markets) and consider incentives to shift customers toward the higher-margin Store Brand
risks: If customers perceive the price increase as too steep they may reduce purchase frequency or substitute with Store Brand, though brand loyalty makes large-scale switching unlikely
Competitors could respond by cutting prices, though they currently charge more and have no structural incentive to do so
Regulatory or reputational risk from raising prices on health-related consumer staples
next_steps: Pilot a $0.30–$0.50 Advil price increase in a subset of stores to measure volume elasticity before a full rollout
Model the profit impact of different pricing scenarios across all three pain reliever brands
Analyze feasibility and legal permissibility of market-based pricing across the 5,000-store network
Assess potential to grow Store Brand share through targeted promotions or reformulation to close quality perception gap
